 Student loan changes in 2026 reshape repayment, forgiveness and borrowing limits for millions of federal loan holders nationwide
 1 / 12 List slides The biggest student loan changes of 2026, explained List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 21, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Federal student loan rules are shifting more sharply in 2026 than at any point in more than a decade. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, rewrites how borrowers repay what they owe. It also resets how much students and parents can borrow in the first place, and how long repayment runs before a remaining balance is written off. Most of the law's major provisions take effect on July 1, 2026. That turns the months before that date into a planning window for anyone carrying federal student debt or about to take some on.
 The student loan changes landing in 2026 are structural, not cosmetic. The Repayment Assistance Plan, an income-driven option known as RAP, becomes the default for new borrowers. It replaces the SAVE plan, which spent much of the past two years frozen in federal litigation. Grad PLUS borrowing ends for new loans. Parent PLUS loans, which for decades could stretch to a school's full price, now run into a fixed limit. Graduate and professional students hit annual and program-level caps for the first time. The menu of income-driven repayment options shrinks to two.
 Three groups feel this most directly. Borrowers already enrolled in SAVE, PAYE or income-contingent repayment need to know when their plan goes away and what replaces it. Prospective graduate students and the parents of undergraduates have to recalculate how much federal money is actually within reach. The gap between published tuition and federal borrowing capacity is widening at higher-cost schools. Anyone pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness needs to confirm whether the payments they have already made still count.
 What follows walks through 10 specific changes, from RAP's payment formula to the deadlines attached to switching plans. It also covers the tax question hanging over forgiven balances. The law is written and the effective dates are set. The work left for borrowers is figuring out which rules apply to them, and when.
 The Repayment Assistance Plan replaces SAVE 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Repayment Assistance Plan, known as RAP, becomes the income-driven repayment option for borrowers who take out their first federal student loans on or after July 1, 2026. Payments are set as a share of adjusted gross income on a sliding scale that rises with earnings, rather than one fixed percentage applied to everyone.
 RAP is built differently from the plans it supersedes. It requires a minimum monthly payment even from borrowers reporting very low or no income, a departure from SAVE, which allowed qualifying borrowers to owe nothing in a given month. Each payment also directs a set portion toward principal, a design meant to curb the balance growth that frustrated borrowers on earlier income-driven plans whose payments were smaller than the interest accruing each month.
 The plan covers federal direct loans for undergraduate and graduate study alike. The payment formula does not shift with degree level, so a borrower holding a master's degree and one holding a bachelor's degree who earn the same income land on the same monthly figure, even when their balances differ sharply.
 Marriage changes the math. Borrowers who file joint federal tax returns have spousal income folded into the figure used to set the payment, mirroring how several existing income-driven plans treat married filers. Couples weighing joint versus separate filing now have a repayment variable to consider alongside the tax bill.
 The plan comes out of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, which rebuilt the federal repayment menu rather than adding to it. Anyone entering repayment after mid-2026 cannot choose SAVE, PAYE or income-contingent repayment instead, because those plans stop accepting new enrollees on the same date. The realistic choice narrows to RAP and income-based repayment.
 For students borrowing for the 2026-2027 academic year, the RAP income scale becomes part of the borrowing decision itself. Where an expected starting salary falls on that scale sets the monthly payment, since the formula keys off income rather than the size of the balance.
 SAVE, PAYE and ICR close to new borrowers in July 2026 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Three income-driven repayment plans — SAVE, PAYE and income-contingent repayment — stop accepting new enrollees on July 1, 2026. After that date, the only income-driven choices for someone entering repayment are the Repayment Assistance Plan and income-based repayment, the single older plan the overhaul leaves intact.
 Closing enrollment is not the same as canceling the plans outright. Borrowers already signed up are not pushed out overnight. The Department of Education is winding the three plans down on a staggered schedule rather than moving every account on one day, and enrolled borrowers will eventually have to shift into RAP or income-based repayment. No universal cutover date applies to everyone. Two borrowers with nearly identical loans can receive transition notices months apart.
 SAVE reached this point after two years of legal turmoil. Federal court orders blocked central pieces of the plan starting in 2024, and borrowers already enrolled were moved into an interest-accruing forbearance while the litigation played out. Payments stopped, balances kept growing, and that forbearance stretch generally did not count toward loan forgiveness or toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Anyone who spent that period in SAVE should assume the clock was not running unless a servicer record shows otherwise.
 PAYE and income-contingent repayment follow the same closure path without the courtroom history. Current enrollees can generally stay put until the wind-down reaches their account, while new sign-ups end in mid-2026. The practical weight falls on people who graduate, leave school or re-enter repayment after that point, because they inherit a shorter menu of options than classmates who started repaying a year earlier.
 Comparing the two surviving plans before that window closes is the practical move. Pulling a current payment history and running the numbers under RAP and income-based repayment shows how a monthly bill and a forgiveness date would change. Starting early leaves room to weigh the tradeoffs rather than accepting whatever plan a servicer assigns by default.
 Grad PLUS loans disappear for new borrowers 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Graduate and professional students lose access to Grad PLUS loans for periods of enrollment that begin on or after July 1, 2026. The program, which let students borrow up to a school's full cost of attendance, stops issuing new loans after that date under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
 Grad PLUS filled a specific gap in federal aid. Direct unsubsidized loans carry fixed annual limits that fall well short of tuition at most medical, dental, veterinary and law schools. Grad PLUS covered the rest — tuition, fees, housing, books — as long as the school certified the amount and the borrower cleared a basic adverse credit check. That made it the main way many students paid for expensive professional degrees without going to private lenders.
 The elimination is not retroactive. Borrowers who already hold Grad PLUS debt from disbursements made before the cutoff keep those loans on the terms they originally agreed to, including the interest rate set at disbursement and the repayment and forgiveness rules that attach to federal direct loans. Only new borrowing is affected.
 Students partway through a multi-year program face the harder version of the problem. Someone who used Grad PLUS for the first two years of a four-year degree cannot keep drawing on it for the remaining years once the program closes to new enrollment periods. The funding source they planned around stops mid-degree.
 What replaces it is a capped system built on direct unsubsidized loans, with defined annual and aggregate limits that differ for standard graduate programs and professional degree programs. Anything above those ceilings has to come from elsewhere — institutional scholarships, assistantships, family money, employer support or private student loans, which carry their own underwriting standards and lack the income-driven repayment and forgiveness protections that federal loans provide.
 Anyone weighing graduate programs for the 2026-2027 academic year should map out funding for the full length of the degree before enrolling, rather than assuming the borrowing capacity earlier cohorts had still exists.
 New borrowing caps hit graduate and professional students 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Graduate and professional students face annual and aggregate caps on federal direct loans starting with the 2026-2027 academic year. The limits are tiered — students in professional degree programs can borrow more than students in standard graduate programs, but both now have a ceiling.
 The tiering tracks a real cost gap. Medical, dental and law programs usually charge tuition well above what a master's program in education or public policy costs, so the professional-degree ceiling sits higher. It remains a fixed figure, though, rather than one that rises with whatever price a school publishes.
 The aggregate limits carry as much weight as the annual ones. They apply across an entire graduate or professional education rather than resetting each year, so a student who borrows close to the maximum early in a four-year program can reach the lifetime ceiling before the final year. Borrowing has to be mapped across the full degree rather than one award letter at a time.
 Caps themselves are not new to federal lending. Undergraduates have borrowed under annual and lifetime limits for decades. Applying the same structure to graduate and professional study changes the math, because the amount of federal credit available no longer moves with what an individual program charges.
 The shortfall will be largest at high-tuition private institutions, including medical and law schools in expensive metropolitan areas, where tuition alone can pass the federal ceiling before housing, health insurance and living costs enter the figure. Students there will have to close the gap with institutional aid, scholarships, family money or private loans. Private loans are underwritten on credit and lack the income-driven repayment options and forgiveness pathways attached to federal debt.
 Anyone comparing graduate programs for 2026-2027 can ask admissions and financial aid offices how the capped federal amount compares with each program's published cost of attendance, and how much institutional grant aid the program typically awards.
 Parent PLUS loans get borrowing limits for the first time 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Parent PLUS loans carry defined annual and aggregate borrowing limits starting July 1, 2026, ending a long stretch in which a parent could borrow up to a school's full published cost of attendance minus other aid. A statutory ceiling, not a credit check, now sets the outer edge of what a family can take on.
 The limits apply per student rather than per parent. A family with two children enrolled at once faces a separate ceiling tied to each child, not a single pool to split between them. Borrowing disbursed before the new rules take effect is untouched. Parents who financed a student's freshman and sophomore years under the old terms keep those loans as written, though any further borrowing for that student's remaining semesters falls under the new ceiling.
 The effect lands hardest at expensive schools. Parent PLUS has functioned for years as the instrument that closes the distance between a dependent undergraduate's own federal direct loan limits and the full bill at a private college or an out-of-state public university. Once the cap binds, that gap does not vanish. It shifts to home equity lines, private education loans, institutional payment plans, or a different enrollment decision.
 Repayment terms for parents stay narrower than the options available to students. Parent PLUS borrowers are not eligible for the Repayment Assistance Plan, the income-driven option that becomes the default for new student borrowers. Their choices remain standard repayment or, through a federal direct consolidation loan, income-contingent repayment. A parent and a child carrying comparable balances can end up with very different monthly obligations.
 Families comparing financial aid offers for the 2026-2027 academic year can ask admissions and financial aid offices for a net price breakdown that reflects the new Parent PLUS ceiling, rather than relying on an older sibling's award letter or a prior year's estimate. The math that covered a 2023 or 2024 enrollee may leave a shortfall for a student starting in fall 2026.
 Forgiveness under RAP now takes 30 years 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Borrowers repaying under the Repayment Assistance Plan reach forgiveness of any remaining balance after 360 qualifying monthly payments — 30 years. SAVE forgave remaining debt after 20 to 25 years, so the new plan extends the wait by five to 10 years.
 SAVE set forgiveness at 20 years of qualifying payments for borrowers whose loans funded undergraduate study, and 25 years for anyone carrying graduate debt. RAP applies a single timeline to everyone. A borrower who financed only a bachelor's degree and a borrower holding six figures of professional school debt now share the same 360-payment clock.
 The practical effect turns on the ratio of balance to income. Borrowers earning well relative to what they owe will often clear the debt outright long before year 30. RAP payments rise with income instead of following a fixed amortization schedule, so the forgiveness provision never comes into play for them.
 The people who actually reach payment 360 are those whose earnings stayed low against a large balance. For that group, the wait stretches out by half a decade or more.
 Anyone who built a payoff date around SAVE's schedule should rerun the math. A borrower who entered repayment in their late 20s under a 20-year timeline expected relief in their late 40s. The same borrower under RAP waits until their late 50s.
 How a forgiven balance gets taxed is unsettled. A federal provision enacted during the pandemic exempted discharged student debt from federal income tax, and that exemption lapsed at the end of 2025. Unless Congress restores it, amounts forgiven through income-driven repayment could count as taxable income in the year of discharge. On a large balance, that would mean a substantial one-time bill. State tax rules are separate and vary. Borrowers nearing the end of a repayment term should take the question to a tax professional well before the discharge date rather than assuming the relief arrives tax-free.
 Deferment options shrink for new borrowers 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Anyone whose first federal student loan is disbursed on or after July 1, 2026 loses access to economic hardship deferment and unemployment deferment. Both pauses have been fixtures of the federal system for decades. Relief for those borrowers runs instead through the Repayment Assistance Plan's income recertification process.
 The logic is that RAP already scales a monthly payment to adjusted gross income and pushes it toward a small fixed minimum when earnings collapse. A borrower who loses a job recertifies income, and the payment drops. A separate status that halts payments entirely becomes redundant under that design.
 A reduced payment and a suspended payment are not the same thing. Economic hardship deferment let eligible borrowers stop payments for up to three years in total, and on subsidized loans the federal government covered the interest accruing during the pause. Unemployment deferment provided a parallel pause tied to job loss. Both stopped the bill outright. Recertification lowers a payment rather than halting it, and servicer processing is rarely instant.
 The result is a split system defined by one variable: when a borrower first took out federal debt. Those with loans disbursed before July 2026 generally keep the deferment and forbearance options that existed under the earlier rules, even after they move into new repayment plans. Two people with comparable balances, loan types and jobs can end up with different relief available to them, separated only by a disbursement date years in the past.
 Borrowers who already hold federal loans and borrow again after July 2026 should ask their servicer which rules apply. The cutoff keys to the first disbursement, not the most recent one.
 The distinction is easy to miss and worth confirming with a loan servicer rather than assuming. Students finishing school in 2026 and 2027 who expect uneven early-career income should understand what changed before signing a master promissory note. The cushion available when earnings fall is narrower than what earlier graduating classes could use.
 Public Service Loan Forgiveness survives, with adjustments 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Public Service Loan Forgiveness remains intact under the 2026 overhaul, and payments made on the Repayment Assistance Plan count toward the 120 qualifying payments the program requires. Borrowers working full time for a government agency or a qualifying nonprofit can still reach forgiveness after a decade of payments.
 The program's architecture is unchanged. A borrower needs federal direct loans, full-time work for an eligible employer, and 120 qualifying monthly payments made under an eligible repayment plan. Eligible employers include federal, state, local and tribal government agencies, 501(c)(3) nonprofits, and some other nonprofit organizations that deliver qualifying public services. Employment must be certified, and a borrower who leaves all of that certification until year 10 can struggle to document old jobs.
 The narrowing plan menu is what changes the picture. Once SAVE, PAYE and income-contingent repayment close, public service borrowers will generally make their qualifying payments under either RAP or income-based repayment. Both count toward the 120. What differs is the monthly amount, which turns on income and family size.
 Progress already earned does not reset at a plan switch. Someone moving from SAVE to RAP, or from income-based repayment to RAP, keeps every qualifying payment already logged, as long as the loan type and the employer stay eligible. The count follows the borrower rather than the plan.
 The SAVE litigation is the complication. Borrowers held in the interest-accruing forbearance that followed the court rulings in 2024 and 2025 generally did not earn qualifying payments during that stretch, so some who assumed they were near 120 are further back than they think.
 Independent records are worth keeping. The PSLF Help Tool on the Federal Student Aid website confirms employer eligibility and displays a current qualifying payment count, and it is worth checking during the 2026 transition rather than trusting that servicer records moved over cleanly.
 What current SAVE borrowers need to do next 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Borrowers enrolled in SAVE should log into their servicer account now and confirm their current status. The next step is comparing what a monthly payment would be under the Repayment Assistance Plan against income-based repayment. No single national deadline triggers the switch, and no SAVE borrower falls into default because the plan is being wound down.
 Verification comes first. Check three things on the servicer's site: whether the account is still sitting in forbearance, whether interest is accruing on the balance, and which repayment plan the account is scheduled to move into. Servicing contracts have shifted between companies in recent years, and accounts have moved with them, so a borrower should not assume every notice and email arrived. Silence from a servicer does not mean nothing is pending.
 The comparison comes second. RAP and income-based repayment use different payment formulas and different forgiveness timelines, and the plan with the lower monthly bill is not always the plan that costs less over the life of the loan. The loan simulator on StudentAid.gov is built for that calculation. Borrowers should rerun it once it reflects the 2026 rules rather than work from figures produced under the old plan lineup.
 Documentation comes third. Ask the servicer for a written qualifying payment count before any plan transition, then keep it. Payment histories have been difficult to reconstruct after borrowers move between plans or between companies, and the months spent in SAVE-related forbearance during the 2024 and 2025 litigation generally did not count toward forgiveness, which complicates the tally further.
 Timing matters most for anyone close to a forgiveness threshold under the older plans, because a transition can change which payments count and when the count picks back up.
 Borrowers who wait until a servicer assigns them a plan lose the chance to run these numbers on their own terms. A placement into standard repayment can produce a far higher monthly bill than an income-driven option would, particularly for borrowers whose balances are large relative to income. Choosing early leaves room to recertify income, switch plans, or correct a servicer error before payments restart.
 The 2026 deadlines every borrower should track 
 Illustration: Quartz
 July 1, 2026 is the date that governs almost everything in this overhaul. It marks the start of the new borrowing caps for graduate, professional and Parent PLUS loans, the end of Grad PLUS loans for new borrowing, and the cutoff after which no one can newly enroll in SAVE, PAYE or income-contingent repayment.
 One date does not cover every deadline a borrower faces. The wind-down of SAVE for people already enrolled runs on a staggered schedule rather than a single universal cutoff, and the timing can vary by loan servicer. The Department of Education has not set one uniform transition date, so checking the account directly with the servicer is the only reliable way to learn when a specific plan change takes effect.
 Families applying for aid for the 2026-2027 academic year should read spring award letters closely. Those letters need to reflect the new graduate, professional and Parent PLUS limits. An award package that still assumes Grad PLUS borrowing or open-ended Parent PLUS eligibility is built on rules that no longer apply, and the financial aid office should be asked to reissue it before any enrollment deposit is due.
 Borrowers close to a 20- or 25-year forgiveness mark under an older plan have a narrower task: confirm the qualifying payment count in writing before any plan change goes through. Payment tallies have proved hard to reconstruct after loans move between servicers or borrowers switch repayment plans, and a written record captured before the switch is easier to defend than one assembled afterward.
 Tax season belongs on the calendar too. The temporary federal exemption that kept forgiven student debt from counting as taxable income expired at the end of 2025. How forgiven balances are treated from here depends on Internal Revenue Service guidance and on whether Congress acts. Anyone expecting a discharge in 2026 or later should raise it with a tax preparer well before the balance is forgiven rather than after a bill arrives, since the amount involved can run into tens of thousands of dollars.
